title: Łuków Landsmen Abroad: Keeping a Community Together
summary: The book’s landsmen associations show how people who left Łuków continued to support one another and remember the town across borders.

## A hometown carried across the ocean

For Łuków’s emigrants, leaving town did not mean leaving its people behind. In New York and elsewhere, former residents formed associations that joined practical support to the work of keeping a shared hometown alive in memory. Their story, as told in *Sefer Łuków*, is not one organization’s uninterrupted history, but a network: societies in America, a postwar landsmanshaft in Belgium, a committee working on housing in Israel, and survivors gathering to remember the murdered.

The memorial book’s account, translated into English by JewishGen, places the beginnings of one New York organization in December 1910. The precise day is unclear in the book’s text; its account says an organization was formed at a Friday evening meeting. A separate passage refers to members joining a Łuków association in 1916. These dates need not contradict each other: the book appears to describe more than one organizational milestone or name, rather than a single cleanly documented founding sequence. Its chapter, “The Łuków Landsmanshaftn in the United States,” is the principal account for this history. ([The Łuków Landsmanshaftn in the United States](/communities/lukow/records/event_candidate_37cda609cd65e0fdf22bd5c1); [Łuków Association](/communities/lukow/records/mention_4f98f3074d10cb23aa25de91); [memorial book, JewishGen translation](https://www.jewishgen.org/Yizkor/lukow/Lukow.html))

The broader history helps explain why such societies mattered. Landsmanshaftn—hometown associations formed by immigrants from the same place—often offered mutual aid and fellowship to people adjusting to a new country. One JewishGen community-history page describes common services elsewhere as sick benefits, burial plots and loans; that general description is context, not proof that every Łuków society supplied every service. ([Anyksciai landsmanshaftn](https://kehilalinks.jewishgen.org/anyksciai/landsmanshaftn.htm)) Łuków’s organizations belong to a much wider pattern of migrant communities sustaining ties across distance. In this case, the memorial book names specific people, institutions and projects that give that pattern a local shape.

## Societies, members and mutual support

The book records a Łuków Society associated with the [Federation of Polish Jews in America](/communities/lukow/records/mention_02485bf05eb584e66e8ff3ad) and the [American Jewish Congress](/communities/lukow/records/mention_e20d1d6fd6d52a0c6d80abdb). It describes medical assistance and community support, and names [Morris Zuckerman](/communities/lukow/records/mention_5cc3b5e44fadfeff7fc023dd) as a leader during a period of development. [Morris Levitt](/communities/lukow/records/mention_6c692e8b4d698a51d2aeeafd), a lawyer, is connected with the society and with the federation; the book also associates him with the legalization of an association. The records do not establish that every reference to Morris Levitt, Morris Levitt/Levit and Marim Levit is certainly the same person, so the name variants should be treated cautiously.

The book preserves a roll of members of the Łuków Association: Gdalye (Joe) Feltsman, Marim Levit, Yudel Flug, Yudel Woland, Simkha and Nisen Hershberg, Chaim Grinboim, Leibl Batshan, Mendel Arlinski and Sidney Hershberg. A second list of society members includes Morris Levitt, Moses Zuckerman, Eli Jannstein, Leibl Rozenboim, Abraham (Albert) Braun, Abraham Glazman, Gdalya (Joe) Feldzman, Abe and Jack Braun, and Dorothy Zweig (Levitt). The similar names Feltsman and Feldzman may reflect spelling variation, but the evidence supplied does not prove that the entries refer to one person. Nor should the two lists be collapsed into a single roster: they appear under different organizational names in the memorial book.

One neighboring body was [Łuków Branch 153, Independent Order of Workers](/communities/lukow/records/mention_b00b4f208c51a4b6d88b372a), which the book says was established in New York in 1931 and collaborated with the society. Together with the federation’s doctors’ district, these links suggest that the landsmen’s work was not isolated: hometown ties could connect members to wider Jewish civic and aid organizations. The book names federation figures including Jacob Brown, Louis Rosenbaum, Dora Levit, Moses Fishbein and Albert Brown. It gives us names and affiliations, but not a complete account of the society’s finances, membership size or the precise medical services provided.

## Help across borders

The memorial book’s account extends beyond New York. It says that survivors formed a Łuków landsmanshaft in Belgium after liberation, and identifies [Israel Goldgewicht](/communities/lukow/records/mention_50f87b92e0075e79e087f8a3) as its leader. The same record connects Goldgewicht to Toybe Berknwald, their son Abraham, and his sibling Leyzer, as well as to migration to Belgium. These family details matter: the postwar organization was built by people whose lives had been scattered by persecution and war. The book’s brief account does not tell us what the Belgian group did day to day, or whether its membership included other branches of Goldgewicht’s family.

Another initiative joined support for living survivors to the rebuilding of life in Israel. The book reports that a Łuków committee, headed by Morris Levit, paid $2,400 to the Joint to help construct two small homes there. ([Łuków housing initiative](/communities/lukow/records/event_candidate_181bfaa08e97ffe95af31615)) This is a concrete figure and a concrete purpose, though the memorial text, as presented in the record, does not identify the recipients, the homes’ location or their eventual residents. It describes a committee acting through the Joint Distribution Committee, linking former neighbors’ contributions to housing assistance in a new country.

That work took place against the destruction of the community they had left. Yad Vashem’s Encyclopedia of the Ghettos describes Łuków’s wartime Jewish population, the forced arrival of Jews from other towns, and the deportations and killings of 1942–43. Its chronology and figures do not always match other summaries exactly: it reports around 5,000 deported on October 5, 1942, and gives separate totals for subsequent deportations and murders. These records establish the scale of the catastrophe independently of the memorial book’s account of the emigrants’ later aid. ([Yad Vashem, Łuków ghetto entry](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/yv/he/research/ghettos_encyclopedia/ghetto_details.asp?cid=529)) The broader town history likewise notes that only a small number of Łuków Jews survived, many having left for the Soviet Union. ([History of the Jews in Łuków](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Jews_in_%C5%81uk%C3%B3w))

## Remembrance after destruction

The societies’ work was not only material. In Rüdesheim, survivors organized a memorial evening for the victims of the Łuków ghetto. The memorial book calls those remembered *kedoshim*—martyrs—and records the gathering as an act of commemoration, not simply a meeting of an association. ([Memorial evening for Łuków ghetto victims](/communities/lukow/records/mention_5b7de93e42b7d29cbc6361ac)) The book also describes a decision to establish a Łuków landsleit association at Alter Hitlmacher’s house and names Eli Yangstitz among those involved. ([Founding of the Lukow Landsleit Association](/communities/lukow/records/event_candidate_f6375ac21e6396d81507b5da); [Eli Yangstitz](/communities/lukow/records/mention_648cd04771770dc0fe7bc788)) These accounts should not be forced into one timeline: the records refer to different places, groups and moments, including wartime remembrance and postwar organizing.

The book’s lists and short notices cannot provide a complete census of Łuków’s survivors or emigrants. A name missing from its pages is not evidence that a person or family had no connection to the town; the memorial volume reflects the memories and documents available to its contributors. Still, the names it does preserve—committee workers, association members, organizers and relatives—show how community endured in altered form. Aid, housing, medical support and memorial gatherings were different tasks, but they shared a purpose: sustaining obligations to people from Łuków, and refusing to let the murdered disappear into anonymity.
